prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val][adversarial] Feature matrix with long row headers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Capability" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 411px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 36px
  col 3: header "Team" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 4: header "Business" · longest unbreakable word 72px · one-line width 72px
  col 5: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 83px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 510px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 509px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A plan-comparison feature matrix: readers check whether a capability exists in each of four plans (Free → Enterprise), so the primary task is scanning a row rightward and comparing the tick/dash pattern across plans, with the capability name as the anchor.","reading":"Readers enter on the left row header, read the capability phrase as a unit, then sweep across the four mark columns to find the first plan that includes it. Vertical comparison of the mark columns is secondary but matters for 'what does Enterprise add' questions. The four mark columns are read as a set, not individually.","groups":["Columns 2–5 (Free, Team, Business, Enterprise) form one visual family: same role (boolean presence), same content type (✓/—), same alignment, and they should share a similar width rhythm so the marks form clean vertical columns and the header row reads as a plan ladder.","Column 1 (Capability) stands alone as the row identifier and must be visually dominant over the mark family."],"keep_intact":["All four plan headers — 'Free', 'Team', 'Business', 'Enterprise' are single unbreakable words (36/44/72/83px), so their columns cannot be narrower than word+21px padding (57/65/93/104).","The longest unbreakable word in column 1 (91px) — column 1 must stay at least ~112px so no word overflows.","✓ and — marks must never be split or clipped; they need only a few px of text width, so their columns are governed by header width, not content."],"may_wrap":["Capability phrases in column 1 — they are multi-word noun phrases that wrap cleanly at spaces, and row height can absorb 2–4 lines without breaking row integrity.","Nothing else: the mark columns contain no wrappable text (headers are single words, cells are single glyphs)."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [166, 63, 71, 99, 110] · table 510×553px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 118, 118, 92] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1B: widths [178, 59, 67, 95, 106] · table 506×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [158, 66, 76, 98, 110] · table 509×580px · row heights [39, 118, 92, 118, 118, 92] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r1A","good":"All five headers stay on one line and the mark columns are comfortably wide, so no tick is crowded. Column 1 at 166px still holds the shortest capability phrases on two lines and the table reads as a proper matrix.","problems":"Three rows fall to four lines and the table is 553px tall, so the five rows no longer scan as comparable units — the eye loses the tick pattern between row 1 and row 4. The plan ladder is also lopsided: Free (63) is barely more than half of Enterprise (110), so the spacing between ticks accelerates left to right.","cause":"Free/Team/Business/Enterprise are given 63/71/99/110, which is 6/6/6/6px above their header minimums (57/65/93/104) — roughly 24px spent on columns whose content is a single glyph — and that width is taken directly out of column 1, which drops below the width needed to keep the long phrases at three lines."},{"design":"r1B","good":"The best of the three: column 1 at 178px (157px text) is the widest, so the tallest cell is only three lines and the table is 474px — rows read as units and the tick pattern is easy to follow down the Enterprise column. Headers intact, no mid-word splits, hyphen break in 'four-hour' is legitimate.","problems":"The mark columns still carry 2–11px of dead width (59/67/95/106 versus 57/65/93/104), and the table only sums to 506 of the 509px available, so 11px that belong to the row header are being wasted. The tick rhythm is still uneven (gaps of 63/81/100px between mark centres).","cause":"Mark columns were sized slightly above their header words for comfort rather than at the header minimum, and the 3px of leftover width was left unassigned instead of being handed to column 1."},{"design":"r1C","good":"The mark family is the most even of the three (66/76/98/110), and Enterprise gets enough room to look unhurried; headers all fit on one line.","problems":"Column 1 at 158px (137px text) is the narrowest of all three, so three rows break into four short fragments and the table balloons to 580px — the tallest and least scannable version. 'Granular role-based access control for workspaces' becomes a four-line stack of stubs, which defeats the row-header anchor role.","cause":"Free and Team were given 66 and 76, i.e. 9 and 11px above their 57/65 minimums, for headers that are only 36 and 44px wide; that 20px came straight out of column 1 and pushed it below the three-line threshold."}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"tight-max","widths":[188,58,66,93,104],"change":"Take the mark columns down to their header minimums (58/66/93/104, i.e. 1px of slack) and hand every recovered pixel to the row header: column 1 becomes 188px (167px text), the widest achievable given that Enterprise cannot go below 104. This is the theoretical maximum for keeping capability phrases at three lines, which keeps the table at its shortest and the tick rows closest together for vertical comparison."},{"name":"balanced-max","widths":[184,59,67,94,105],"change":"Same strategy as tight-max but with a 2px safety margin on each mark column so sub-pixel rounding can never wrap a header, at a cost of only 4px from column 1 (163px text). Safer refinement of r1B: recovers the 11px r1B wasted while keeping a little air around 'Free' and 'Team'."},{"name":"ladder-air","widths":[180,57,68,96,108],"change":"New idea: keep column 1 at a solid 159px text width (still three lines, as r1B proves) and spend the remainder on a deliberately widening ladder — Free pinned to its 57px minimum, Team 68, Business 96, Enterprise 108. The extra room goes to the right end, where the tick is densest and where readers look for the 'what does Enterprise add' answer, so the last two mark columns don't feel pinched next to the long row headers."}]}
